title: Evolution with an LLM as the mutator

questions.text: Why can no heuristic score below 0% excess over the L1 bound?
options: The sandbox rejects any program that scores below 0%
The evolve set is too small for a rule to beat L1 on it
L1 = ⌈total size / capacity⌉ is the fewest bins any packing could use, and the packer checks that every item is placed and no bin overflows
Best fit is optimal for online packing, so nothing can beat it
questions.explain: Bins hold at most their capacity, so the total size divided by the capacity, rounded up, is a floor. A rule that seems to beat it must lose items or overfill a bin, and task.check_packing rejects both; it runs in the parent process, which the candidate cannot reach. Best fit is not optimal: our evolved rules beat it.

questions.text: Which of these does the module's sandbox turn into a failed candidate rather than a score? Pick all that apply.
options: import os in the program
A while True loop
Scores containing NaN
Scores containing −inf
Returning one score per bin that ranks bins like best fit
questions.explain: The screen rejects imports other than numpy and math; the CPU limit and timeout stop endless loops; NaN fails the packer's check. −inf is allowed, because argmax still picks a bin, and a best-fit clone is a valid program: it just scores the same as best fit.

questions.text: One draw between two clusters: best fit at 4.781% excess and first fit at 5.340%. With T = 0.25 points, what share of such draws (in %, nearest whole number) picks best fit's cluster?
questions.explain: p = 1 / (1 + exp(−(5.340 − 4.781) / 0.25)) = 1 / (1 + e<sup>−2.236</sup>) ≈ 0.90. At T = 2.5 it would be about 0.56: a higher temperature means less selection pressure. The loop itself draws two parents from two different clusters, so an island with only two clusters always gives both, and T starts to matter from three clusters on.

questions.text: Over 3 seeds of 400 candidates each, what did the evolution loop's kept programs gain over best fit on the 10 held-out instances?
options: 0.35 points on average: about 0.52 in two seeds and 0 in one
Nothing in any seed
More than 2 points in every seed
It lost to best fit in every seed
questions.explain: Held-out gains were 0.520, 0.000 and 0.517 points (mean 0.35 ± 0.30). Seed 1 never found anything better than best fit on the evolve set, so it kept a best-fit twin.

questions.text: Random search over a small expression grammar, with no LLM and the same 400-candidate budget, did what?
options: It never produced a valid program
It matched evolution exactly in every seed
It beat evolution on all three sets
It beat best fit on the evolve set in 2 of 3 seeds, by less than evolution on average, and its seed-0 program packed the shifted instances far worse than best fit
questions.explain: Random search gained 0.19, 0.31 and 0 points on the evolve set (evolution: 0.62, 0 and 0.31). On the shift set (sizes 20–100, bins of 150) its seed-0 program scored 10.71% against best fit's 5.01%: it fit the Weibull sizes, not packing in general.

questions.text: In the 'LLM, no selection' control, every prompt shows only first fit and best fit. What did its seed-0 run keep after 400 candidates?
options: A rule 0.6 points better than best fit
Nothing valid
Best fit's behaviour: no child beat 4.781%
First fit
questions.explain: Its best child used exactly best fit's bins. 36% of its candidates were exact repeats. Without children becoming parents, the LLM kept circling the textbook rule it was shown.

questions.text: Without a verifier, each child became the next parent untested. What happened in seed 0?
options: Children kept raising exponents and constants (powers of 400, then 10,000; terms like 1e18) until scores overflowed to NaN; 299 of 356 children failed and none beat best fit
It improved steadily, like the loop with a verifier
It stopped after the first failure
It found the same rule as evolution seed 0
questions.explain: Asked each time for a version 'better than every version above', the model escalated the numbers in its own last guess. Nothing checked them, so from about child 57 on almost every child returned NaN. The checker is what turns a stream of guesses into a search.

questions.text: What do the best evolved and random-search rules have in common, read from their code?
options: They are best fit with a different tie-break
They always open a new bin for large items
They sort the items before packing
A term like 1/(room left + 1e-8) gives an exact fit a huge score; otherwise they lean toward bins with more room
questions.explain: Sizes are whole numbers, so room left after an exact fit is 0 and 1/(0 + 1e-8) is 10<sup>8</sup>. For any other bin that term is at most 1, and added terms such as 0.1·√bins or log(bins + 1) favour roomier bins. Online packing cannot sort: items arrive in order.

questions.text: One extra run drew parent clusters uniformly instead of by score (T = ∞), seed 0. How did it compare?
options: It never left best fit
Its best program, at 4.035%, beat every by-score seed (best 4.159%)
It crashed on most candidates
It equalled the by-score mean exactly
questions.explain: We expected the opposite (E9, missed). One seed proves little, but at 400 candidates strong selection may narrow the search too early: in seed 1 the by-score loop spent its budget around best fit and found nothing.

questions.text: OpenEvolve 0.4.0, run for 100 iterations with the same local model and our evaluator, ended with what?
options: A rule better than all of ours
No valid program at all
Best fit itself: all 68 valid programs it stored used exactly best fit's bins
A program that failed the held-out check
questions.explain: Of 103 programs it stored, 68 were valid and every one of them packed exactly like best fit; the rest failed. At this budget and with this model, the library did no better than our 'no selection' control.
